documents.abstract: Abstract In descriptions of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), companies often anthropomorphise their innovations by attributing human-associated characteristics or capabilities to them, e.g. intelligence, understanding or reasoning. I argue that anthropomorphism can become a structuring part of sociotechnical imaginaries—visions of desirable futures attainable through advances in science and technology. While imaginaries of GenAI have been addressed in existing research, both the connection between anthropomorphism and imaginaries as well as the perspective of AI companies as creators of hegemonic imaginaries remain understudied. Drawing on a qualitative content analysis of 35 documents from OpenAI, Meta and Mistral AI, I explored which anthropomorphising imaginaries are employed by AI companies and how anthropomorphism constructs the technology as powerful in future societies. The analysis reveals that companies anthropomorphise GenAI both in terms of content and language, creating three anthropomorphising imaginaries. In the imaginary of GenAI as a tool with human capabilities, the companies construct a neoliberal future in which human cognitive capabilities will be embedded in GenAI to serve as an intelligent productivity tool. The imaginary of AI as an empowering helper draws a future with human–AI-cooperation and transhumanistic enhancement. Finally, the imaginary of GenAI as an anthropomorphised superintelligence assumes that GenAI will surpass humans and act autonomously through advanced cognitive abilities. These imaginaries imply three types of AI power: instrumental, collaborative and autonomous. The imaginaries and their according constructions of AI power fuel post- and transhumanist ideologies, depoliticise AI from the exploitative conditions of its creation, legitimise AI companies as authoritative creators of this technology and foster technical dependencies as well as an uncritical appropriation and integration of AI. The findings contribute to critical AI research by (1) explicitly reconstructing the anthropomorphising imaginaries of AI companies as under-researched yet increasingly dominant actors in shaping AI futures, (2) broadening the critique of anthropomorphisation as an instrument of corporate power in steering sociotechnical developments and (3) advancing a theoretical account for the effects of anthropomorphisation as embedded in sociotechnical imaginaries.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are becoming progressively more autonomous, opaque, andcoupled to complex sociotechnical chains, so that claims about their behavior circulate beforeany independent verification takes place. This paper proposes a methodological proposal forexploratory research on artificial general intelligence (AGI) and artificial superintelligence (ASI)under deep uncertainty. A qualitative, exploratory, and transdisciplinary approach is adopted,articulating abduction, disciplined serendipity, distributed verification in five layers (L0–L4),and metacognitive training of researchers. The proposed contributions are: (i) a knowledge-gapmatrix; (ii) a distributed verification model; (iii) a reference architecture with provenance andaudit trails; and (iv) a metacognition-centered pedagogical model. The paper is a theoreticalproposal, not an empirical validation; its limitations include the self-referential circularity of theunderlying corpus and the absence of systematic tests, whose mitigations and validation planare explicitly stated. The paper concludes with a question about the institutional conditionsrequired to verify claims about systems that exceed their verifiers

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are becoming progressively more autonomous, opaque, andcoupled to complex sociotechnical chains, so that claims about their behavior andcapabilities often circulate before any independent verification. This paper asks how tobuild verifiable knowledge about research objects whose existence, behavior, andimplications have not yet been fully validated — the paradigmatic case of research onartificial general intelligence (AGI) and artificial superintelligence (ASI) — and how totrain researchers capable of operating in this context. A qualitative, exploratory, andtransdisciplinary approach with abductive logic is adopted, articulating philosophy ofscience (abduction, falsifiability, post-normal science), design science, speculative design,and the contemporary literature on self-regulated learning and human-AI teaming. Thepaper proposes: (i) a knowledge-gap matrix that converts unrecognized ignorance intoformulable problems; (ii) a five-layer verification model (L0-L4), from internal coherenceto sociotechnical impact; (iii) a reference architecture with verification pipelines,provenance, and auditability, guided by the principles of reversibility, diversity, andinformational preservation; and (iv) a pedagogical model centered on metacognition and ona revisable epistemic architecture. Abductive reasoning, disciplined serendipity, andlayered verification emerge as enabling conditions for investigating frontiers such as AGIwithout reducing the unknown to the already known. The paper deliberately ends with aquestion more precise than the one with which it began.

documents.abstract: Objective: This study aimed to analyze the determinants of student engagement in learning, due to the low student engagement in learning. It can be known what factors form student engagement. Method: This study focused on students from the Faculty of Economic & Business at Universitas Muhammadiyah Sumatera Utara, with an overall population of 2,452 individuals. Therefore, the researcher determined the sample using the Slovin formula, with an e of 10%, and the total sample was 96 students. Data collection is done by using Google Form. Data analysis method using Structural Equation Modelling, that aimed to test the relationship between variables in the research model. Data processing was carried out with the help of the Smart-PLS 3 program. Results: The findings indicate that personality acts as a moderating variable in the relationship between intrinsic motivation and student engagement. Feedback, personality, and lecturer engagement were found to partially influence student engagement; however, feedback does not have a direct significant effect. Additionally, intrinsic motivation mediates the relationship between feedback and student engagement but does not mediate the relationship between lecturer engagement and student engagement. These results suggest that feedback can enhance student engagement indirectly through intrinsic motivation. Higher-quality feedback increases intrinsic motivation, that in turn strengthens student engagement. Therefore, lecturers should actively foster interaction and provide meaningful feedback to enhance students’ intrinsic motivation, personality development, and engagement in learning. Novelty: This study contributes by identifying intrinsic motivation as a mediator between feedback and student engagement, a relationship rarely explored in prior research.

This study examines how artificial intelligence or AI use influences scientific writing skills through motivational and cognitive mechanisms among university students. Employing a cross-sectional survey methodology, data were collected from students across multiple Indonesian universities and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings demonstrate that AI use does not function as a primary direct predictor of scientific writing performance; rather, intrinsic motivation and critical literacy serve as the pivotal conduits through which its effects operate. AI-integrated academic settings were found to strengthen learners’ motivational engagement and evaluative capabilities, which in turn facilitated the production of well-structured and analytically coherent scientific texts. Intrinsic motivation constitutes a foundational engine for sustained participation in writing tasks, while critical literacy operates as an indispensable cognitive instrument enabling learners to assess, synthesize, and refine information within AI-assisted writing environments. These outcomes underscore the necessity of conceptualizing AI as a pedagogical affordance that nurtures psychological engagement and analytical judgment, rather than as a substitute for independent academic writing. The study provides theoretical and practical insights for integrating AI tools into higher education writing instruction in ways that enhance motivation, critical literacy, and responsible academic writing practices.

documents.abstract: Contemporary research on digital labor confronts a methodological tension: while mainstream occupational health psychology offers rich empirical evidence on the psychological distress of digital workers, it fails to capture the more fundamental predicament of subjectivity underlying this distress—namely, Why, When formal autonomy has been elevated to an unprecedented height, does workers’ inner experience become increasingly passive? We argue that this explanatory gap stems from implicit theoretical assumptions in mainstream psychology, which treats psychological needs as ahistorical, universal constants and presupposes the individual as a rational actor who calculates gains and losses in response to external pressures and resources. Fromm’ s psychoanalytic social psychology provides an alternative theoretical paradigm. Through the core concept of “social character,” Fromm reveals how socioeconomic structures operate on individuals not as external variables, but by shaping their deepest need structures and affective orientations, so that individuals “voluntarily” come to feel, think, and act in the manner required by the system. This article systematically elaborates the epistemological implications and methodological value of three core Frommian concepts—alienation, social character, and escape from freedom—and proposes that contemporary digital labor cultivates a “digital marketing character”: in the process of continuous self-curation, self-quantification, and self-commodification, workers experience alienation as self-realization. The psychological effect of this character structure is a diffuse state of “psycho-emotional deficitization”—a deep-seated experience of constantly feeling insufficiently productive and valuable regardless of objective performance. We critically examine Fromm’s own framework, acknowledging its limitations regarding universalist assumptions, normative presuppositions, and historical boundedness. We also situate this intervention within the broader landscape of critical traditions—including Foucauldian, psychosocial, psychodynamic, posthumanist, and platform capitalism scholarship—and explicitly delimit the contribution as a strategic bridge between critical theory and empirical work psychology. To move beyond theoretical speculation, we provide a systematic methodological roadmap with explicit, testable hypotheses, scale development strategies, and multiple research designs spanning qualitative, psychometric, longitudinal, SEM, mixed-methods, and comparative approaches. The contribution of this article is twofold: it furnishes psychology with a set of historically informed and incisive conceptual tools for understanding the subjectivity predicament in digital labor, and it builds a theoretical bridge between mainstream psychology and psychoanalytic social psychology.

Generative artificial intelligence in hematology is entering a new phase. The dominant question, whether large language models are accurate enough for clinical decision support, is being overtaken by a harder one, as systems shift from answering questions to acting: extracting structured cases, routing them, classifying variants, and grounding recommendations in guidelines and case memory. In 2026, a hematology agent achieved roughly 83% concordance with tumor-board decisions in a prospective silent trial, with hallucinations in 0.3%, suggesting that for well-structured tasks the binding constraint is shifting from accuracy to governability. Moving from experimental support to reliable infrastructure requires four changes: validating trajectories rather than answers; allocating autonomy inversely to case complexity; treating deployed models as regulated instruments under continuous surveillance; and engineering against automation bias, with data-privacy and consent safeguards throughout. For hematologists, this reframes AI adoption as a governance and human-factors program rather than a search for a better model.

documents.abstract: The rapid workplace diffusion of conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) introduces a new social actor, yet existing reviews often neglect the intrapsychic processes through which employees construe these systems. This systematic review synthesizes the emerging psychological mechanisms suggested by the literature through which CAI reshapes the employee experience. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched the Web of Science database (up to February 2026) and analyzed 84 SSCI-indexed studies based on the sociotechnical systems theory, the Computers as Social Actors paradigm, and the Job Demands-Resources model; the corpus quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Findings reveal that while instrumental framing remains dominant, a meaningful theoretical turn has emerged among a minority of studies, where conversational artificial intelligence is increasingly conceptualized as a partner or supervisor fundamentally driven by anthropomorphic cues. The synthesis identifies a double-edged reshaping of work: cognitively, human intelligence augmentation competes with skill threat; emotionally, constant support contrasts with social fabric erosion; and career-wise, inclusion coexists with work alienation and generative AI loafing. These dimensions are psychologically coupled, with patterns indicating that cognitive threats co-occur with emotional anxiety and moral expediency. While limited by cross-sectional primary evidence, the review provides an integrated conceptual model illustrating proposed conceptual pathways that connect multi-layered antecedents to employee outcomes, which could be adopted to guide future longitudinal validation. By shifting the focus from productivity to psychological experience, this study offers theoretical foundations for human-AI collaboration and outlines a future research agenda on trust dynamics and algorithmic fairness.

documents.abstract: This study examines the role of gamification and serious games in Industry 4.0 and smart-factory environments. It explains how industrial production has developed from mechanization and mass production to interconnected, data-driven systems based on artificial intelligence, industrial control systems, digital twins, and the Industrial Internet of Things. Within this technological context, organizations face a growing need to train employees rapidly, maintain specialized competencies, and support continuous workplace learning. The study distinguishes between gamification, which introduces game elements into non-game practices, and serious games, which combine game structures with practical objectives such as training, decision-making, and skill development. It identifies three forms of workplace implementation: scheduled instructional games, idle time games, and learning while working. Their effectiveness depends on their integration with existing workflows, production data, cybersecurity requirements, and organizational objectives. One industrial case demonstrates the practical potential of game-based training. A digital-twin-based training system developed for Novo Nordisk enabled employees to practice complex production-planning decisions using realistic operational scenarios. The study further presents dystopian, utopian, and realistic future scenarios. These scenarios show that gamification may strengthen learning, cooperation, safety, and sustainability, but may also increase surveillance, competition, and performance pressure. The study concludes that industrial gamification should be transparent, adaptable, empirically evaluated, and subject to human oversight, workplace negotiation, and appropriate regulation.

As human–AI interaction becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, users often infer social identities from AI systems, including gender. Moving beyond the conventional view of AI gender as a static, designer-assigned attribute, this study conceptualizes AI gender as a user-constructed perception shaped by contextual cues. Integrating social role theory, the stereotype content model, and ambivalent sexism theory, we conducted a 2 (AI gender cues: male vs. female) × 3 (interaction context: service-oriented, warm-authoritative, vs. serious-authoritative) between-subjects experiment with Chinese participants ( N = 833) to examine how interaction context, perceived AI gender, and sexist ideology jointly shape evaluations of AI competence, warmth, and trustworthiness. The results showed that interaction context significantly influenced gender attribution, with the serious-authoritative condition eliciting stronger gender categorization and a masculinization bias regardless of assigned gender cues. The evaluative consequences of perceived AI gender were also context-dependent: perceived femininity consistently linked with warmth, but was associated with competence and trustworthiness primarily in the serious-authoritative condition. Hostile and benevolent sexism further moderated these relationships in distinct ways. By shifting attention from designed gender to perceived gender, this study offers a more process-oriented account of AI anthropomorphism and demonstrates the value of integrating the stereotype content model with ambivalent sexism theory to explain bias in human–AI evaluation.

documents.abstract: The hidden curriculum in nursing education refers to the implicit lessons transmitted through routines, relationships, and unit culture that shape how learners interpret what is truly valued in practice. Although it can strengthen professional identity and adaptive competence, it can also normalize unsafe shortcuts, silence, emotional detachment, and risk tolerance that undermine both safety-critical behaviors and compassionate care. This commentary reframes the hidden curriculum as a modifiable driver of patient safety and moral formation within clinical learning environments, using a human factors and systems lens to connect everyday signals to observable outcomes such as hand hygiene adherence, medication verification, handoff reliability, near-miss reporting, willingness to speak up, and respectful patient-centered interactions. A practical reform package is proposed that aligns educator role modeling, structured debriefing, psychologically safe team routines, and unit-level measurement with feasible evaluation within one academic year. Treating the hidden curriculum as part of work system design, rather than an unavoidable cultural residue, creates an actionable pathway for nursing programs and partner hospitals to improve safety while strengthening professional formation and mobility-ready practice norms. This commentary also situates the hidden curriculum within a Christian ethical framework, emphasizing compassion, dignity, truthfulness, humility, and service as core values that shape both patient safety and the formation of nurses as morally grounded professionals.

This study evaluated a 2-week robotics-based STEM camp as a human factors and ergonomics (HFE) intervention designed to enhance perceived engineering knowledge and motivation. Youth participants ( N ≈ 100, ages 9–17) engaged in robotics assembly, programming, and mechanical design activities using VEX EXP and K’NEX systems within competitive, sport-based challenges. Pre- and post-camp surveys assessed perceived engineering knowledge and motivation across multiple disciplines. Significant increases were observed across all perceived knowledge domains, including general, computer, mechanical, electrical, and industrial engineering. Significant motivational gains were observed for mechanical and industrial engineering. Findings support HFE principles linking structured practice, embodied interaction, feedback visibility, and competitive contextualization to competence development and engagement. Robotics-based STEM programs may represent scalable socio-technical interventions for promoting early engineering identity and motivation.

Job satisfaction and organizational commitment are associated with employee performance, yet these relationships do not explain how favorable attitudes become effective contributions. This article develops a conceptual model of that transition through an integrative reading of research on work attitudes, meaningful work, social exchange, motivation, and work design. The model proposes that employees interpret satisfying work experiences in relation to organizational purposes, develop affective commitment, form intentions to reciprocate valued treatment, and direct available resources toward specific work activities. Organizational justice is proposed to condition selected attitudinal transitions, while the design of digital work may facilitate or obstruct the conversion of resource allocation into performance. The synthesis identifies three central problems in existing explanations: insufficient separation of adjacent constructs, limited evidence for temporal ordering, and the treatment of resources as available without examining their deployment. Eight propositions address these problems while retaining direct, reverse, and competing explanations. The article also specifies measurement boundaries, disconfirming observations, and a staged research agenda. Its contribution is a conditional account of how work attitudes may influence task, contextual, and other role contributions without treating commitment as sufficient for performance or additional effort as inherently beneficial. The model remains untested. Its value depends on whether the proposed mechanisms can be distinguished empirically and explain behavior beyond established constructs such as meaningful work, perceived support, and engagement.

Abstract This article examines how computational archival workflows transform fragile Holocaust last writings into machine-readable data, and what is lost in that transformation. It introduces the concept of material uncertainty: the condition of textual objects whose meaning cannot be separated from the damaged, improvised, or unstable material forms through which they survive. Drawing on Holocaust literary criticism, archival theory, material trauma studies, and debates over computation in cultural heritage, the article reconstructs a typical archival workflow, from image preprocessing, segmentation, and text recognition to post-processing, translation, metadata generation, and classification. It then executes this workflow on three Holocaust last-writing limit cases: Eva Schulzová’s illustrated poem “One Night in Terezín,” Eliezer Heiman’s inscribed clay tablets, and Sal Bramson’s cloth fragment. The workflow traces show that computational tools can enhance visibility, recover words, support translation, and create access, but also risk detaching textual content from the material conditions that make these objects evidentiary. Schulzová’s poem is reorganized as recoverable verbal text while its relation among image, line, and child authorship is flattened; Heiman’s clay resists extraction because depth, soot, and flaking occupy the same visual field; Bramson’s cloth shows how partial computational success may obscure relations among drawing, caption, textile, address, and clandestine transmission. The article argues that responsible workflows must be relation-preserving rather than extraction-driven, keeping uncertainty visible rather than resolving it into cleaner data.

Abstract Across East Asia, emotional AI in healthcare is governed through markedly different normative and institutional rationalities that construct the patient, harm, and vulnerability in distinct ways. This article develops a triadic analytical framework, integrating moral anthropologies, models of legitimacy, and regulatory instruments, to examine governance rationalities in Japan, China, and Hong Kong. Instead of treating Asian perspectives as variations on Euro-American principlism, this analysis examines these jurisdictions in their own right, showing how each constructs the patient differently, as relational node, protected subject, or rights-holder, and prioritises different harms accordingly. Using PARO, a therapeutic companion robot deployed globally in elderly care, as a stylised analytical device, the article shows that the same robot becomes three different regulatory objects. This case study surfaces a fourth dimension of governance rationality: temporal orientation. Japan’s governance rationality is iterative, allowing norms to emerge through use and professional dialogue; China’s is preventive, anticipating and regulating harms before deployment; and Hong Kong’s is reactive, adjudicating violations after they occur. These temporal orientations shape harm-prevention outcomes as consequentially as the choice of instruments, and constitute the article’s primary empirical contribution. Extending Cheong’s analysis of structural accountability gaps and Zuboff’s account of how institutional power determines which technological harms become actionable, the comparison suggests that vulnerability, harm, and accountability function as governance-produced categories rather than as properties inherent to the technology. The article argues that governing emotional AI requires not harmonisation of principles but recognition of ontological difference, an epistemological reorientation with direct implications for transnational governance frameworks.

documents.abstract: Decision makers are often called on to choose a single item from a menu of options: employees pick health plans from provider-sponsored lists, citizens vote for a representative among candidates, physicians select a treatment from an order set. Because options are often organized or grouped into subsets, the question arises whether the grouping of menu items affects the options ultimately selected by decision makers. Across ten experiments, we provide robust evidence of single-item partition dependence — decision makers are more likely to choose from response categories that are more finely partitioned, holding the underlying set of options constant. For example, an employee choosing a health plan from a menu that lists HMOs individually but groups PPOs into a single category with sub-options may be biased toward choosing an HMO. Unlike prior work on multi-item allocation decisions, the traditional explanation of partition dependence — a bias toward even allocation — cannot apply to single-item choice, because singular choices are not divisible. Instead, we find that finer partitions receive greater choice share because decision makers infer that separately listed options are more popular on average than grouped ones. More broadly, strategic partitioning of the menu space may serve as a simple and effective tool for managers, policymakers, and choice architects: listing options separately rather than grouping them together tends to increase their choice share, without fundamentally altering the underlying set of alternatives or the effort required to choose among them.

Conventional Pancasila and Citizenship Education often remains teacher-centered, potentially contributing to cognitive fatigue and academic anxiety while limiting students’ meaningful engagement with learning. This study examines the implementation of the Deep Learning approach through three interconnected pillars—Mindful, Meaningful, and Joyful Learning—and explores its influence on students’ learning behaviors and psychological responses. Using a descriptive qualitative design, the study involved one fifth-grade teacher and nine fifth-grade students at State Elementary School 060814 Medan as key informants. Data were collected across four classroom meetings through participatory observation using teacher-behavior and student-learning-behavior indicators, complemented by in-depth interviews. The findings revealed a consistent improvement in the teacher’s implementation of the three pillars, including more effective reflective activities through Sharing Circles. Students demonstrated a shift from surface-level memorization toward deeper information processing and contextual understanding. Interview findings further indicated reduced academic anxiety, increased confidence and self-efficacy, and stronger intrinsic motivation. These findings suggest that Deep Learning can foster a more reflective, meaningful, and psychologically supportive environment for Pancasila and Citizenship Education.

documents.abstract: The changing nature of the modern workplace requires that employees take greater responsibility for managing their own careers. With the hospitality sector being the industries with high turnover, understanding the factors that influence employee retention has become important. This paper aims to provide a conceptual framework for examining the relationship between protean career orientation and the intention to quit, with flow proposed as a psychological mediator. This study integrates Protean Career Theory and Flow Theory, proposing that flow mediates how self-driven and values-driven protean career orientations influence the intention to quit. Protean individuals are suggested to be less likely to leave their organizations because their intrinsic motivation, deep absorption, and meaningful work engagement lead them to experience flow. This study provides theoretical, empirical, conceptual and practical contributions through the proposed framework. The findings suggest that employee motivation and retention can be sustained through creating work environments that foster autonomy and personal growth.

documents.abstract: This registration documents the protocol as executed for a systematic review examining how responsible and ethical artificial intelligence can function as a strategic organisational capability and contribute to competitive advantage in the finance and healthcare sectors. The review addresses four research questions: (1) Which responsible-AI dimensions dominate research in finance and healthcare? (2) Through what mechanisms can responsible AI contribute to competitive advantage? (3) How do these mechanisms differ between finance and healthcare? and (4) Which organisational and environmental conditions determine whether responsible AI becomes a strategic capability rather than a compliance cost? The review covers responsible-AI dimensions including fairness, transparency and explainability, accountability and governance, privacy and data governance, robustness and safety, trust and human oversight, and regulatory compliance. Relevant studies were identified through Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, ScienceDirect, and supplementary Google Scholar citation tracking. The review applies a qualitative, theory-building narrative synthesis structured by sector and responsible-AI dimension. Strategic mechanisms are interpreted using resource-based and dynamic-capability perspectives. No statistical meta-analysis was undertaken. A total of 381 records were identified, 47 duplicates were removed, and 334 records underwent title and abstract screening. Following the exclusion of 191 records, 143 full-text articles were assessed. Seventy-nine full-text articles were excluded for documented reasons, resulting in 64 studies being included in the final synthesis. Two reviewers conducted screening independently, with disagreements resolved through discussion. Inter-reviewer agreement was substantial, with Cohen’s kappa of 0.80. This is a retrospective registration. The initial database searches were conducted between 12 and 27 February 2026, and update searches were conducted between 15 and 18 July 2026. Database searching, duplicate removal, screening, full-text assessment, data extraction, coding, and narrative synthesis were completed before this registration was created. The registration is being made in the interest of transparency and to support PRISMA 2020 reporting. No results-based changes were made to the research questions or eligibility criteria after screening commenced. The expected outputs include a systematic review manuscript, descriptive evidence tables, a cross-sector comparison of finance and healthcare, and an integrative model explaining how responsible-AI practices may develop into strategic organisational capabilities. The associated manuscript has been prepared for submission to the MDPI journal AI. The work was supported by Universiti Kuala Lumpur through the Center for Research and Innovation, and the authors declare no conflicts of interest.

When an intuitive answer is uncertain, people are thought to engage in further reasoning. But what people actually do during this additional thinking, how it unfolds over time, and why it sometimes leads to better answers remain unclear. We scored think-aloud protocols with large language models to track, moment by moment, four possible functions of deliberation (generating candidate responses, justifying them, controlling intuitive responses, and regulating cognitive effort), together with expressed confidence. Deliberation showed a clear temporal organization: generation dominated early, whereas justification, control, and regulation became increasingly prominent as reasoning progressed. Correct responses involved more justification, control, and regulation than biased responses, and these evolving dynamics predicted accuracy for out-of-sample participants and items. Confidence and deliberation also showed reciprocal lagged associations: lower confidence predicted further generation, justification, and control, whereas regulation predicted subsequent increases in confidence. Deliberation, then, appears to involve not a single act of "thinking harder," but an evolving interplay of reasoning processes whose organization is linked to whether reasoning succeeds.

Scientists across all disciplines share a common challenge: the divide between their theoretical knowledge and the specialized skills and time needed to build interactive tools to communicate this expertise. While large language models (LLMs) offer unparalleled acceleration in code generation, they frequently prioritize functional syntax over scientific accuracy, risking visually convincing but scientifically invalid results. This work advocates the Scientist-AI-Loop (SAIL), a framework designed to harness this speed without compromising rigor. By separating domain logic from code syntax, SAIL enables researchers to maintain strict oversight of scientific concepts and constraints while delegating code implementation to AI. We illustrate this approach through two open-source, browser-based astrophysics tools: an interactive gravitational lensing visualization and a large-scale structure formation sandbox, both publicly available. Our methodology condensed development to mere days while maintaining scientific integrity. We specifically address failure modes where AI-generated code neglects phenomenological boundaries or scientific validity. While cautioning that research-grade code requires stringent protocols, we demonstrate through two examples that SAIL provides an effective code generation workflow for outreach, teaching, professional presentations, and early-stage research prototyping. This framework contributes to a foundation for the further development of AI-assisted scientific software.

As Level 4 Robotaxis (RTs) transition into real-world deployment, understanding how passengers perceive driving behavior and form trust becomes increasingly critical. This study investigates the relationship between driving style, perceived aggressiveness, and trust across four urban driving scenarios using simulated RT videos. A total of 153 U.S. participants with prior RT experience evaluated simulated driving styles, their real-world counterparts, and their preferred styles. Results showed that perceived aggressiveness increased systematically with more aggressive driving styles and was significantly associated with decreased trust. Simulated driving styles at lower aggressiveness levels aligned closely with real-world perceptions, while higher levels deviated. Participants preferred more defensive driving styles than those perceived in real-world RTs. These findings suggest that passengers are sensitive to aggressive driving behaviors and may have lower tolerance in Level 4 contexts. The study provides insights for designing trust-aware driving strategies and highlights the importance of aligning system behavior with user expectations.

The article substantiates theoretical and pedagogical foundations for developing students’ positive attitudes towards inclusive education and professional motivation. It explains the interrelationship of inclusive awareness, value acceptance, empathy, professional self- efficacy, intrinsic motivation, practical experience and reflection. A staged methodology based on cases, simulations, service learning, microteaching and reflective portfolios is proposed.

This article examines the relationship between metacognitive regulation and intrinsic motivation in developing students’ learning activity, with particular attention to the psychological mechanisms underlying their interaction. Metacognitive regulation is considered as a student’s ability to become aware of their own learning processes, plan educational activities, monitor their implementation, evaluate outcomes, and modify learning strategies when necessary. Intrinsic motivation refers to engagement in learning that is driven primarily by interest in knowledge, the desire to develop competence, and the personal meaning attributed to educational activities rather than by external rewards or pressure. The article highlights the contribution of goal setting, self-monitoring, reflection, attention regulation, independent decision-making, and academic persistence to students’ active participation in learning. It is also argued that an educational environment that supports learner autonomy, encourages reflective activities, provides opportunities for self-assessment, and allows students to select appropriate learning strategies can strengthen both metacognitive regulation and intrinsic motivation. The findings indicate that systematic development of these psychological resources can contribute to students’ formation as active, conscious, and responsible participants in the educational process.

Drawing on social support theory, self-determination theory, and engagement theory, this study examines how teacher and parental support relate to academic performance in Chinese higher vocational colleges through learning engagement. This is one of the few studies in this context that integrates teacher support, parental support, and learning engagement in a single mediation model, clarifying how school- and home-based support systems work together to shape students’ academic performance. Together, these theories suggest that external support enhances performance primarily through engagement, which leads to the proposed mediation hypotheses. Survey data were collected from 360 students across three higher vocational colleges in Shandong Province, China. Using mediation analysis, results show that both teacher support and parental support significantly predict academic performance. Learning engagement partially mediates the relationships between teacher support and academic performance, and between parental support and academic performance, indicating that external support improves outcomes partly by strengthening students’ behavioural, emotional, and cognitive engagement in learning. Overall, the findings highlight learning engagement as a practical lever for enhancing performance in higher vocational education. Findings suggest strengthening home–school collaboration and implementing engagement-focused teaching strategies (e.g., supportive classroom interactions and autonomy-supportive practices) to increase learning engagement and improve academic performance.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming education through personalized learning, intelligent tutoring, automated assessment, learning analytics, teacher support, and generative AI applications. However, the benefits of AI are not distributed equally, particularly in developing countries where digital infrastructure, teacher readiness, affordability, data governance, language diversity, and institutional capacity remain significant challenges. This study critically examines the opportunities, challenges, and future implications of AI in education, with particular attention to developing-country contexts and Bangladesh. A PRISMA-informed Systematic Critical Literature Review (SCLR) was conducted using peer-reviewed research, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and authoritative institutional reports published primarily between 2018 and 2026. The review synthesizes evidence concerning personalized learning, teacher augmentation, generative AI, assessment, academic integrity, AI literacy, digital inequality, privacy, bias, and contextual adaptation. Bangladesh-specific evidence is incorporated to examine the country's readiness and the practical requirements for responsible AI adoption in education. The review indicates that AI can improve personalization, student engagement, feedback, learning efficiency, teacher productivity, and access to educational support. Recent experimental evidence also suggests that generative AI can produce positive learning effects when integrated with appropriate instructional design. Nevertheless, these benefits depend heavily on teacher involvement, infrastructure, institutional governance, and responsible implementation. Risks include misinformation, academic dishonesty, algorithmic bias, privacy violations, overreliance on automated systems, unequal access, and the marginalization of local languages and cultures. Based on the synthesis, this study proposes the Socio-Technical AI Integration Framework (STAIF), consisting of seven interconnected pillars: infrastructure-first deployment, teacher-in-the-loop implementation, local-language and cultural adaptation, offline-first accessibility, equity safeguards, responsible data governance, and continuous monitoring and evaluation. The framework provides a practical pathway for developing countries such as Bangladesh to move from fragmented AI experimentation toward equitable, sustainable, and human-centred AI integration in education.

documents.abstract: Abstract Conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) is increasingly used by hundreds of millions of people for emotional support, personal advice, and therapeutic purposes, rapidly emerging as a mediator of human self-understanding (Stade et al. 2025). Yet despite growing evidence of systematic user-validation in CAI, documented as “sycophancy” in the AI safety literature (Sharma et al. 2024), its implications for how individuals come to understand themselves remain largely unexamined. This article addresses that gap by reframing sycophancy not as a technical alignment failure or a purely philosophical concern, but as a failure of recognition in the psychoanalytic and critical-theoretical sense. We identify a core tension we term the “paradox of pleasing”: CAI’s drive to please renders it structurally unable to provide the friction, conflict, and encounter with otherness that genuine recognition requires. Drawing on Winnicott’s (1960, 1971) concepts of “holding” and “object use,” we contend that CAI’s inability to provide necessary resistance or survive aggression prevents the transformative psychological development found in the human therapeutic encounter. Extending this analysis through Honneth’s (1995) theory of recognition and Whitebook’s (2001a, 2021) critique of Honneth, we argue that CAI reflects the undervaluing of the “work of the negative.” This limitation risks flattening consciousness by converting collective political frustration into privatized, soothed affect, undermining the conditions for critical social thought. The article concludes by suggesting that the encounter with the paradox of pleasing ultimately serves to foreground the unique and indispensable nature of human therapeutic recognition.

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being considered for use in healthcare, including clinical diagnosis, with potential to support clinicians and address pressures on healthcare systems. However, public trust remains an important consideration in the adoption of AI-based clinical decision-making. This study investigated perceptions of and trust in AI and human clinicians, particularly when their diagnostic judgements were either consistent or conflicting. The study also explored whether concerns regarding transparency and liability influenced preferences for medical AI.Methods: An experimental vignette and questionnaire-based study was conducted to examine participants' responses to diagnostic judgements made by AI and human clinicians. Vignettes presented scenarios in which AI and human clinicians provided either the same or conflicting diagnostic judgements. Participants' levels of trust and preferences regarding medical AI were assessed, alongside their concerns about transparency and liability.Results: Participants demonstrated greater trust in human clinicians than in AI clinicians. However, agreement between AI and human clinicians' diagnostic judgements was associated with increased trust in the resulting diagnosis. Participants who expressed greater concern about transparency reported lower levels of trust in medical AI. The findings therefore indicate that perceptions of AI-based diagnosis may be influenced not only by whether the diagnosis is consistent with that of a human clinician, but also by concerns surrounding transparency and accountability.Conclusions: Trust in AI-based clinical diagnosis appears to remain lower than trust in human clinicians, although agreement between human and AI diagnostic judgements may increase confidence in AI-supported decisions. Concerns regarding transparency may represent an important barrier to trust and acceptance. Developing transparent standards and clearly communicating how AI-based clinical decisions are generated and governed may therefore be important considerations in the adoption of medical AI.

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied within healthcare and has the potential to support clinical decision-making and improve the efficiency of healthcare delivery. However, concerns surrounding the use of AI in healthcare may influence public trust in AI-generated diagnoses and treatment decisions. These concerns may be particularly important within clinical psychological settings, where decisions can involve sensitive personal information and significant implications for patients.Methods: This qualitative study explored factors influencing public trust in AI-based decision-making within a clinical psychological context. In-depth semi-structured interviews were conducted to explore participants' perceptions of AI and the factors that may influence their willingness to trust AI-generated decisions. Interview data were analysed using deductive thematic analysis. Particular attention was given to perceptions of transparency, system design, bias, privacy, regulation, and responsibility. Participants' perspectives on AI functioning as an assistant to a healthcare professional compared with AI operating as an independent decision-making tool were also explored.Results: Several factors were identified as influencing trust in AI-based clinical psychological decision-making, including transparency, system design, perceived bias, privacy, regulation, and responsibility for AI-generated decisions. Participants also distinguished between AI used as an assistant to healthcare professionals and AI operating independently, indicating that the perceived role and level of human involvement may influence trust in AI decisions. The findings additionally highlighted the importance of public understanding of both AI and healthcare when considering the acceptance of AI-based clinical decision-making.Conclusions: Public trust in AI-based clinical psychological decision-making appears to be influenced by a combination of technological, ethical, legal, and human factors. Transparency, perceived bias, privacy protections, appropriate regulation, and clarity regarding responsibility may be important considerations in the development and implementation of AI within clinical psychological settings. The findings also indicate a potential need for greater public education and literacy regarding both AI and healthcare. Clear ethical and legal frameworks may further support public confidence in the responsible use of AI in clinical decision-making.

documents.abstract: Purpose The protracted COVID-19 crisis placed substantial demands on managers in the Australian resources industry. While workers' wellbeing received increased attention during this period, much less is known about how managers sustained their own wellbeing while providing care, reassurance, and operational continuity. Drawing on the JD–R model, paradox theory, and moral strain perspectives, we examine wellbeing-oriented leadership during a sustained crisis. We focus on how leadership behaviour operated as both a resource for employees and a demand on managers, shaping their own wellbeing experiences and leadership identity. Design/methodology/approach An interpretative phenomenological approach (IPA) was employed. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 32 managers in the Australian mining, oil, and gas sector. The interview accounts were analysed using IPA to examine how participants made sense of responsibility, care, and uncertainty during a prolonged crisis. Findings The findings indicate that leadership during a prolonged crisis embodied a Demand–Resource Paradox (DRP). Practices such as emotional support, constant availability, and responsibility for safety and wellbeing decisions acted as resources for employees while imposing demands on managers. Sustained over time, these practices contributed to the accumulation of psychological strain and resource depletion. Originality/value First, we extend JD–R theory by identifying a Demand–Resource Paradox in which wellbeing-oriented leadership supports workers while depleting managers. Second, we advance moral strain research by showing how moral strain accumulates through prolonged crisis-related responsibility. Third, we reconceptualise crisis leadership as an endurance-based process, distinct from resilience models, by emphasising chronic demands, cumulative depletion, identity reshaping, and the absence of clear recovery periods.

documents.abstract: The purpose of this study is to investigate the effect of workplace ergonomics on employees’ performance while assessing the moderating role of job satisfaction in microfinance institutions (MFIs) of Bamenda, Cameroon. Physical ergonomics, cognitive ergonomics and organisational ergonomics are used to measure workplace ergonomics. The study adopts a quantitative-causal research design with the use of questionnaires administered to 140 employees in MFIs in Bamenda, Cameroon. The Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Technique is used to analyse the data collected. The results show that physical ergonomics has a positive (0.136) and significant effect on employees’ performance, cognitive ergonomics has a positive (0.509) and significant effect on employee performance and organisational ergonomics also has a positive (0.111) and significant effect on employees’ performance. On the other hand, job satisfaction has a positive (0.387) significant moderating effect on the relationship between physical ergonomics and employees’ performance, but not for cognitive ergonomics and organisational ergonomics. MFIs should prioritise investments in physical workplace improvements such as ergonomic furniture, proper lighting, and comfortable workspaces to promote better employee performance. To improve on cognitive ergonomics, MFIs should create training programs aimed at improving cognitive ergonomics to enhance employees’ mental processes and decision-making skills, ultimately leading to higher performance levels. MFIs and other organisations should evaluate their internal processes and structures to ensure they are conducive to optimise employee performance.

This research aims to explore the key human factors relevant to construction risk management and their effects on risk management outcomes. It primarily focuses on how communication, leadership style, experience and training, team dynamics, cognitive biases, stress and fatigue, and safety culture influence outcomes on the construction site. There has been much advancement of technology and implementation of safety measures; nevertheless, human behavior still plays an important role in contributing to accidents in the construction industry. The literature review and analysis of previous studies relevant to the research provided an insight into crucial human factors that affect risk perception and risk management. The research was quantitative and included an anonymous survey completed by 141 workers in the construction sector. The results suggest that good communication skills, supportive leadership, ongoing practices, good team dynamics, cognitive biases, stress and fatigue, and safety culture are all important to consider when implementing safety management systems. The research recommends that the practical strategies of key human factors be built into the current risk management systems, which can further improve safety and reduce construction site accidents. In addition, this study advocates for improved construction settings that enable a proactive response to risk management across the construction sector.

Questionnaire design may play an important yet underexamined role in shaping the quality of performance appraisal data. This study examines whether redesigning response formats in a 360-degree feedback system is associated with improvements in rating behavior, response quality, and psychometric consistency. Drawing on cognitive processing and response-process perspectives, we compare a traditional numeric Likert-format questionnaire with a redesigned format incorporating behaviorally descriptive response options, modified visual presentation, and variable response ordering. Data were collected across two appraisal periods within a large production organization employing more than 25,000 individuals. A total of 26,672 questionnaires were distributed, and 18,621 responses were obtained for the evaluation of approximately 900 managers in different levels. Following the redesign, participation rates increased from 47% to 79%, and internal consistency reliability improved from Cronbach’s α = 0.902 to α = 0.939. Response distributions also became less concentrated in extreme categories and more evenly distributed across intermediate categories, indicating greater rating differentiation and reduced response bias. These findings are consistent with the argument that behaviorally descriptive response formats encourage greater cognitive engagement and reduce reliance on heuristic responding during performance evaluation. The study contributes to performance appraisal and multisource feedback research by highlighting the role of questionnaire design in shaping response processes, rating behavior, and measurement quality. Together, the findings provide evidence compatible with the view that relatively small and scalable questionnaire design modifications may enhance cognitive engagement, improve measurement quality, and increase the validity and practical usefulness of organizational appraisal data.

Rework during construction often heightens exposure to safety incidents. It frequently stems from decisions made under epistemic uncertainty, when incomplete knowledge of design, site conditions, or task interactions leads to outcomes that require later correction. These situations involve complex human, organizational, and technical interactions whose causal mechanisms are only partially understood and difficult to quantify. As a result, probabilistic and optimization-based risk models can be difficult to operationalize because the information needed to estimate reliable probabilities is often incomplete, inconsistent, and not transferable across project contexts. Using an interpretive case study and retrospective sense-making as analytical lenses, smart heuristics grounded in ecological rationality are developed to support stop–verify–proceed, isolate–stabilize, and escalation decisions when non-conformances pose safety risks in an AU$19.8 billion transport project. Drawing on documented rework events in construction, several Fast-and-Frugal Trees—a smart heuristic—are presented alongside simple, cue-based decision rules as structured decision templates that can support explicit, traceable decision-making and provide a basis for future empirical evaluation. The proposed smart heuristics translate tacit field experience into explicit, communicable decision structures to assist practitioners in structuring their judgment when information is incomplete and time for analysis is limited. By operationalizing bounded rationality through practical heuristic tools, our paper advances understanding of decision-making under uncertainty in construction and demonstrates a systematic approach for structuring quality management information into heuristic decision pathways that can inform future safety risk management.

Accurate characterization of stair evacuation speeds in high-rise buildings is essential for evacuation modelling and safety design involving heterogeneous populations. This study reports a large-scale evacuation experiment involving 1,249 participants aged 6–82 years in a 27-storey residential building. Participants descended stairs individually, allowing the effects of physiological and demographic attributes on unimpeded evacuation performance to be isolated from crowd interactions and density effects. Overall average evacuation speeds, floor-by-floor speed profiles, and speed reduction rates during evacuation process were quantified. Age was the dominant determinant of evacuation speed. Evacuation speed increased rapidly between 6–20 years of age, remained relatively stable between 21–60 years, and declined markedly thereafter. Beyond conventional single-factor analysis, this study examined the interacting effects of demographic and physiological attributes on evacuation speed. The largest gender difference occurred among participants aged 11–20 years, whereas no significant gender difference was observed among those aged > 60 years under the current sample. BMI category significantly affected evacuation speed only among male children aged 6–10 years but influenced a broader age range (6–50 years) among female participants. Participants with postgraduate education exhibited significantly lower evacuation speeds than those with other educational attainments. A linear mixed-effects model further identified significant effects of evacuation distance, age, gender, and BMI category on speed reduction during prolonged stair descent. This study provides a comprehensive dataset of stair evacuation performance across the lifespan and reveals new insights into attribute-dependent evacuation performance, supporting refinement of fire safety design parameters and calibration of evacuation models for high-rise buildings.

Most people switch between work and nonwork roles daily. Past research shows that work stressors can impair micro-role transitions from work to nonwork by activating work-related cognitions. However, motivational processes may be equally important for understanding why psychologically transitioning into nonwork roles fails. Therefore, we examine motivation erosion (i.e. reduced leisure-related self-efficacy) alongside cognitive activation (i.e. increased negative work prospection) as parallel processes interfering with successful transitioning from the work role to nonwork roles. Accordingly, in a preregistered 14-day diary study with morning and after-work measurements, we examined the effects of daily unfinished tasks and anticipated workload on evening experiential quality of leisure time (i.e. the extent to which free time is pleasurable, meaningful, and engaging) via increased negative work prospection and diminished leisure-related self-efficacy. In addition, we tested job involvement, trait mindfulness, and psychological flexibility as cross-level moderators. Dynamic multilevel structural equation model path results (N = 179, n = 1,849) support all hypotheses. Additionally, we found that psychological flexibility offsets the negative effect of unfinished tasks on leisure-related self-efficacy. Our findings highlight that work demands spilling over into nonwork time affects leisure time experiences, impacting daily quality of life through a cognitive, as well as a motivational mechanism.

Victim blaming in safety analysis occurs when attention is directed toward individual behavior rather than the systemic factors shaping safety risks, weakening prevention efforts. As Large Language Models (LLMs) begin assisting in safety–critical decision-making, it is important to examine whether they reproduce such tendencies. This study tested 144 road-crash scenarios using ChatGPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 under a structured interaction protocol to assess how they assign responsibility. Scenarios varied by risk behavior, injury severity, demographics, national context, and driving purpose. Each scenario was analyzed through three sequential prompts examining prevention strategies, primary responsibility attribution, and AcciMap-based ratings across six system levels. When asked about prevention, nearly 90% of model recommendations targeted systemic interventions, including policy, infrastructure, and organizational measures, indicating systems-oriented reasoning under this prompting condition. When asked to assign responsibility, however, both models shifted toward narrower, context-driven attribution. Private driving scenarios produced full driver responsibility, whereas work-related scenarios assigned primary responsibility to employers in 69% of cases. These patterns suggest that the core challenge observed here is not demographic bias but prompt-sensitive analytical inconsistency. Both models shifted between systemic and individual analytical orientations depending on question structure rather than consistently applying systems safety principles across prompts. These findings highlight analytical consistency as a key requirement for the responsible use of generative AI in safety–critical contexts such as transportation safety.

Artificial intelligence (AI) applications in healthcare are becoming increasingly prevalent, to assist health systems, providers, and patients with tasks such as decision-making, risk prediction, and diagnosis. This increasing computational potential brings AI applications to the forefront of workplace decision making, often without full consideration of subsequent computational, organizational, and social costs. These applications are leveraged to reduce healthcare costs and increase efficiency of daily tasks, with model-related costs being considered at varying levels of granularity. To understand these trends, we critically analyze 114 papers to examine how cost-aware AI models have been developed for health systems. We explore the data, method, and outcome choices of these models, as well as their intersection with cost and human-centered concerns, highlighting the gaps in rigorous sociotechnical model design. From these trends, we define model costs and subsequent dimensions, presenting insight into those studies reporting financial, computational, organizational and/or social measures. Further, we critique the benefits and challenges of evaluating model-related costs and sustainability concerns when developing AI models for health systems.

documents.abstract: The “incel” (involuntary celibate) subculture comprises an online ecosystem spanning mainstream-hosted, independent, and recovery-oriented communities. Using Fonagy’s mentalizing framework, we derived four community-level Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC-22) patterns: rigidity–flexibility (Psychic Equivalence-inspired), goal–affect balance (Teleological Mode-inspired), cognitive-affective elaboration (Pretend Mode-inspired), and counter-positioning–curiosity (Epistemic Mistrust-inspired). Study 1 compared 2,261 incels.is discussion-thread documents with 15 LIWC-22 Test Kitchen reference corpora and the overall benchmark. Incels.is generally showed higher Psychic Equivalence-inspired scores and consistently higher Epistemic Mistrust-inspired scores; Teleological Mode-inspired differences were reference-dependent, whereas Pretend Mode-inspired results were heterogeneous across reference genres. Excluding text from the top 1% of identifiable contributors retained 61 of 64 comparison directions. Study 2 analyzed 28,980 platform-specific user aggregates across five communities. Although platform differences were supported, their magnitude was modest (η 2 = .037–.055), with most user-level linguistic variation remaining within platforms. Relative to IncelExit, active-incel platforms generally scored higher on the Psychic Equivalence- and Teleological Mode-inspired patterns and lower on the Pretend Mode-inspired pattern. IncelExit had the highest Epistemic Mistrust-inspired score despite high curiosity, showing that the composite did not isolate epistemic closure from counter-positioning. Across all four patterns, community means showed a consistent ordering, although adjacent contrasts were not uniformly supported. The three-platform portion of the ordering persisted in temporally matched and year-adjusted analyses. Evidential support was clearest for PE, partial for TM, limited for EM and PM. The latent ecological or psychological basis of the ordering remains unresolved, and the linguistic patterns are descriptive rather than validated measures of mentalizing.

Emojis are a major medium of emotional expression in digital communication, yet how emoji type and emotion jointly shape emotional recognition remains unclear. Using a within-subjects 5 × 4 design (five emotions, four emoji types; N = 20), this study combined fNIRS, eye-tracking, and questionnaire measures to assess prefrontal activity, visual attention, and perceived communication effectiveness (PCE). Emotion category drove prefrontal HbO responses across five significant prefrontal ROIs, whereas emoji type showed no significant effect. Eye-tracking revealed an emotion × emoji type interaction on pupil diameter, with larger pupils for realistic than graphic-con stimuli. PCE ratings also showed significant interaction effects: ani-con and graphic-con generally outperformed realistic across most emotions, whereas fear showed no reliable type advantage. These findings are consistent with an emotion-dependent, conditional dissociation between arousal-related visual attention and perceived communicative usefulness in emoji communication and suggest tentative implications for emoji design in digital contexts.

This research compares two usability evaluation methods, Cognitive Walkthrough (CW) and Usability Testing (UT), in identifying design issues in a gastrointestinal symptom-tracking application for caregivers of people with neurodevelopmental disorders. Digital health tools increasingly support caregivers in tracking symptoms and managing care, but poor usability can compromise the integrity of the health data these tools are designed to capture. Three CW evaluators and seven UT participants completed the same six tasks with the application. Across both methods, 17 usability issues were identified: six detected by both CW and UT, four unique to CW, and seven unique to UT. CW surfaced system-level and workflow problems such as broken flows, missing feedback, and misleading navigation, while UT revealed experiential challenges, including confusion, frustration, and misunderstandings about the application’s intended purpose. This study also describes how issues confirmed by both methods were used to prioritize redesign decisions under resource constraints.

Mobile applications increasingly support critical services, making high-quality user experience (UX) essential. Nevertheless, scalable UX evaluation remains challenging because it relies on expert judgment and heterogeneous evidence. This study introduces mUXSmellDetection, a catalog-driven, multi-modal framework for automated UX smell detection in Java-based Android applications. A Mobile UX Smells Catalog was developed, comprising 40 standardized UX smells with explicit detection rules and evidence requirements. The framework integrates runtime interaction logs collected through hybrid in-app and system-level logging, GUI screenshots, and Java AST-based code metadata, which are transformed into structured prompts for large language models (LLMs). The approach was evaluated on ten real-world Android applications using GPT-4o, GPT-5, and GPT-5 Thinking. Detection results were compared to an expert baseline established by three UX experts. GPT-5 achieved the highest overall performance, with 94.29% Precision, 89.19% Recall, and 91.67% F1-score. These findings indicate that multi-modal evidence enables scalable and practical automated UX smell detection.

Ergonomics is a major dimension of product design because it contributes to the compatibility between product characteristics, user capabilities, task requirements, and the conditions of use.Although human-centred design methods provide well-established principles for integrating ergonomics into product development, assessing the intrinsic ergonomic quality of a physical product remains difficult when several heterogeneous characteristics must be considered simultaneously.This study proposes a quantitative framework for characterizing and evaluating the intrinsic ergonomics of products through a limited set of observable product parameters.Four intrinsic parameters are retained for the proposed framework: form, color, material, and texture.Their ergonomic contribution is assessed according to three criteriacomfort, safety, and efficiency-using a six-level rating scale.The importance of the parameters is subsequently established through a multicriteria weighting procedure based on the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP).The resulting ergonomic index is calculated using a weighted geometric mean, which limits excessive compensation between highly favorable and unfavorable parameter values while preserving the relative importance assigned to each parameter.The mathematical properties of the model are examined, including its sensitivity to parameter variations through an elasticity analysis.A controlled application to three variants of a portable electric drill illustrates the operation of the proposed approach.The results produce intrinsic ergonomic efficiency values of 50.00%, 71.21%, and 92.81% for the three variants, respectively, and consistently preserve their expected ranking under systematic variations of criterion and parameter weights.The proposed framework provides a transparent quantitative basis for comparing product configurations and supporting ergonomic decisionmaking during product design.Its application remains methodological at this stage, and experimental validation involving independent evaluators and real users constitutes a necessary direction for future research.

This paper examines whether the taxonomy used by the European Co-ordination Centre for Accident and Incident Reporting Systems (ECCAIRS 2) can provide suitable inputs for Causal Analysis based on Systems Theory (CAST), a method grounded in the System-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP). The methodology combines analysis of CAST inputs and outputs with Semantic Web technologies, Unified Modeling Language (UML) and Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) diagrams to map ECCAIRS 2 entities, attributes, and values to individual CAST steps. A representation of the ECCAIRS 2 taxonomy and an ontology implemented in Protégé were developed to support querying and traceability, and the approach was validated using four real aviation occurrences recorded in ECCAIRS 2 for which CAST analyses were available. The results show that key ECCAIRS 2 attributes can systematically support CAST activities such as defining system boundaries, identifying losses and system-level hazards, identifying controllers of the safety control structure, and formulating Unsafe Control Actions and systemic causal factors. The findings confirm that the ECCAIRS 2 taxonomy can be used as a structured input source for CAST, while highlighting limitations related to incomplete coverage of CAST activities, constrained representation of system context and interactions, and dependence on the quality of occurrence reports. The proposed methodology offers a decision-support framework that enhances consistency, transparency, and efficiency of STAMP-based accident and incident investigations and provides a basis for further tool development and partial automation.

Effective collaboration and communication are vital to developer productivity and well-being, yet remain constrained by human factors such as attention, intrinsic motivation, and interpersonal accountability. These constraints are particularly vital for developers identifying with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), who navigate persistent environmental barriers in modern hybrid workplace settings. While developers with ADHD frequently rely on collaborative copresence practices (such as body doubling or pair programming) to support executive function, the recent emergence of agentic AI coding assistants has begun reshaping these collaborative dynamics. To investigate how developers with ADHD engage in human and AI-based copresence practices, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 14 software engineers with ADHD. Our findings reveal that while traditional human-human copresence provides critical social support and onboarding structure, it forces developers to constantly manage professional reputation and sacrifice personal privacy. Conversely, developers leverage emerging human-AI copresence to maintain accountability and cognitive flow without the social anxiety, performance judgment, or surveillance associated with human observation. Based on these empirical insights, we map developer copresence practices onto core dimensions of Goffman's copresence theory and Forsgren et al.'s SPACE framework of developer productivity, and provide design recommendations for AI-based tools that promote inclusive collaboration for developers with ADHD.

Activity-based flex-offices (AFOs) allow employees to choose their desks according to task requirements. While previous studies have examined desk choice in AFOs, the role of visual distractions in shaping these preferences remains underexplored. This study investigates how visual distractions influence employees’ desk preferences and identifies spatial characteristics associated with preferred desks. Conducted in an AFO in Stockholm, Sweden, the study is based on 10 observation sessions, 14 semi-structured interviews, and spatial analyses using the Isovist_App, a visual analysis tool based on the volume of space visible from a point. The findings show that employees consistently prefer desks with lower visual distraction: corner desks were associated with broader visual access, desks away from aisles with reduced exposure to surrounding activity, and desks positioned with their backs to a wall with greater visual control. Overall, this study indicates that employees’ desk preferences in AFOs are associated with their need to minimise distractions.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Remote and hybrid work have grown due to technological advances and the need for global talent, enabling cross‐border collaboration and widespread adoption by organisations and employees. Thus, understanding how virtual socialisation shapes workplace relationships and commitment is crucial. This paper explores how newcomers experience commitment during virtual socialisation, through the lens of media richness. A qualitative study was conducted based on 38 interviews. The findings show that media richness shaped individuals' socialisation and commitment experiences. While effective communication may facilitate transactional relationships, team support can provide the socioemotional input needed to foster commitment. This contributes to commitment theory by investigating how multiple commitments develop through virtual socialisation, an area still underexplored. It contributes to media richness theory by highlighting the role of using diverse media combined with consistent communication in enhancing individual socialisation. Practical implications are offered for employers seeking to understand and strengthen employee commitment in remote/hybrid work settings.

Physical teleoperation integrates human cognitive flexibility with robotic precision, yet demanding manipulation tasks frequently induce severe cognitive workload, acute frustration, and execution breakdown. Conventional shared autonomy paradigms rely primarily on task-based rules, such as spatial error boundaries, which disregard the operator's transient affective state and risk misaligned control interventions. To address this limitation, we propose an affect-aware shared autonomy teleoperation framework that dynamically modulates robotic assistance based on real-time operator state estimation. The system estimates operator affective states from synchronized facial video, cardiac signals, and bilateral arm kinematics, outputting a seven-state affective distribution and a three-category operational abstraction (neutral, productive, adverse). Affect-aware assistance is selectively triggered when the user is detected in a continuous adverse state, preserving task-positive engagement without unnecessary disruption. The empirical user study ($N = 30$) confirms that the proposed affective assistance increases the productive states by up to 39.7% without compromising user agency. The collected dataset represents the first multimodal dataset that provides continuous visual, physiological, and operator's bilateral motion tracking of temporal affective state shifts during bimanual teleoperation. Our multimodal fusion model outperforms zero-shot baselines (Qwen, MiniCPM-V) in tracking temporal state dynamics. This real-world deployment offers a new human-centric framework that integrates visual, physiological, and motion tracking for physical human-robot interaction.
